The seminar hall at the engineering college held sixty first-years, and Naveen, a final-year, had been invited to talk about his summer internship. He clicked to his first slide. "So basically we built an ETL pipeline feeding an LLM with RAG, deployed on K8s, with CI/CD for the MLOps side."
In the third row, Suraj stopped writing. Around Suraj, pens paused. Someone opened a phone under the desk.
Naveen kept going, faster, pleased with how smoothly it was flowing. "Obviously the latency on the vector DB was the bottleneck."
By minute four, half the hall was looking at the ceiling fans.
At the end there were no questions. Naveen walked out a little annoyed. "Tough crowd," he told the coordinator. "I kept it really basic."

qa.q: How many first-years were in the seminar hall?
qa.a: Sixty first-years.

qa.q: Why did Naveen feel he had kept it really basic?
qa.a: Naveen felt pleased with how smoothly it flowed because those terms were everyday words in his internship, so they seemed basic to him and he couldn't see that first-years had never heard them.

qa.q: What could Naveen have done in his first minute instead?
qa.a: Say in plain words what the project did, with one everyday example, and explain any acronym he truly needed before using it.

qa.q: What was the talk like for Suraj in the third row?
qa.a: Suraj stopped writing almost immediately, likely feeling lost and maybe a bit resentful at being made to feel behind.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming first-years know his acronyms and losing them within the first minute.

passage:
Hi Anjali,
Today's outreach talk at the girls' school was a disaster, and honestly I don't know what more I could have done. I spent two weeks on the slides! I opened with how CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA to find a PAM site, then went straight into off-target effects and HDR versus NHEJ. Standard stuff, it's in every first-year module.
Within a minute the Class 9 students were whispering and one was drawing on her hand. Their teacher kept smiling at me in a tight way. When I asked "Any questions?", one girl said, "What's a gene?" A gene! I nearly laughed.
I think they just weren't interested in science. Should I even bother going back next month?
Elizabeth

qa.q: What did one girl ask when Elizabeth asked for questions?
qa.a: "What's a gene?"

qa.q: Why does Elizabeth think the students just weren't interested in science?
qa.a: The terms feel standard to Elizabeth after a first-year module, so the whispering looks like boredom rather than students lost from the first slide.

qa.q: What should Elizabeth change before going back next month?
qa.a: Start with what a gene is, use a simple picture like editing one word in a recipe, and leave out acronyms unless each one is explained.

qa.q: What might the teacher's tight smile have meant?
qa.a: The teacher may have seen the class was lost from the start and felt uncomfortable, wanting to be polite to the visitor while the lesson wasn't landing.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming school students know the acronyms and background and losing them at once.

passage: Manoj, you missed my film club talk, so let me, Dhruv, tell you how it went. I had fifteen minutes to pitch our short film to the funding committee. First line: "We'll shoot 4K log at twenty-four fps, with a thirty-five mil prime and a gimbal for the oners." I thought that sounded professional. The committee is two economics professors and the canteen manager. Within a minute the canteen manager was checking his watch. One professor asked, "Sorry, what's a oner?" I explained it with more terms. She nodded slowly, the way people nod when they've given up. We got half the money we asked for. I was annoyed at them for days. But I've been thinking... maybe I never told them what the film was even about.

qa.q: Who was on the funding committee?
qa.a: Two economics professors and the canteen manager.

qa.q: Why was Dhruv annoyed at the committee for days?
qa.a: Dhruv thought the talk sounded professional and clear, so the poor result felt like the committee's fault; only later did it occur to Dhruv that they never heard what the film was about.

qa.q: How could Dhruv open the pitch next time?
qa.a: Start with the story of the film and why it matters, in plain words, and bring in camera details only if someone asks.

qa.q: How might the professor have felt asking "What's a oner?"
qa.a: She might have felt a little awkward admitting she didn't know, and when the answer used more terms, she gave up trying to follow.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming a committee knows film terms and losing them in the first minute.

passage:
I'm Gurleen, and I was in the second row for the NSS orientation when Nilesh, our final-year volunteer lead, gave his talk to about eighty first-years.
He opened with: "So this term we continue the WASH audit in Khanpur, finish the DPR, and hand the O&M plan to the SHG as per the SBM guidelines."
I watched the faces around me. The boy next to me looked at his friend. A girl in front wrote "DPR??" in her notebook. Within a minute, three people were on their phones.
Nilesh kept going, faster, clicking through slides of charts. When someone at the back finally asked, "Sorry, what does WASH mean?", he paused and said, a bit sharply, "It's on the first slide," though it wasn't.
Afterwards he told me, "Nobody here even cares." I'm not sure that was true. They just didn't know what he was talking about.

qa.q: What did the girl in front write in her notebook?
qa.a: She wrote "DPR??" in her notebook.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's sharp reply and his comment afterwards suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He seemed irritated and resentful, blaming the first-years for not caring, because the acronyms were so familiar to him that he didn't see he had lost them.

qa.q: What went wrong in the first minute, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: He started with acronyms nobody knew; he could open with one plain story of what the volunteers actually did in Khanpur and explain each short form the first time.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see the first-years' reaction differently from Nilesh?
qa.a: Gurleen thinks they weren't bored or uncaring; they simply didn't understand the words, which is why they drifted to their phones.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming first-years know the acronyms and background, and losing them in the first minute.

passage:
Monday: Siddharth, twenty-one, rehearsed his final-year project talk for Pradeep in the hostel room. "Our CNN hits an F1 of 0.91 on the augmented set, beating the baseline SVM." Pradeep, a history student, asked, "What's an F1?" Siddharth laughed. "Don't worry, the panel will know."
Thursday: The panel had three members. One was the dean of humanities. By the second slide, the dean was frowning at the screen; by the fourth, writing something in the margin. When she asked, "What problem does this solve for a farmer?", Siddharth said, "As I said, the F1 is 0.91," and moved on.
Next Monday: The feedback sheet said "strong technical work, unclear to non-specialists". Siddharth threw it on his bed. "They should have sent a real panel." Then he picked it up again and read the line about farmers twice.

qa.q: What did the feedback sheet say?
qa.a: It said "strong technical work, unclear to non-specialists".

qa.q: Why does Siddharth feel resentful about the feedback?
qa.a: He was so sure his terms were common knowledge that the panel's confusion feels like their failing, not a gap in how he explained it.

qa.q: At which point could Siddharth have caught the problem early, and what would help?
qa.a: On Monday, when Pradeep asked what an F1 was; he could have treated that question as a warning and opened with the farmer's problem in plain words.

qa.q: What was the presentation like for the dean of humanities?
qa.a: The dean was probably lost from the second slide and frustrated when her direct question about farmers got a number instead of an answer.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming the panel knows the acronyms and background, losing them early, and resenting the result.
